---
title: "Vertical layout"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 9,
  out.width = "100%",
  dpi = 150,
  dev = "ragg_png"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(forestmap)
```

By default the forest plot sits above the heatmap and each study is a
column. With many studies the plot gets wide. `orientation = "vertical"`
turns it on its side, like a traditional forest plot: each study is a row,
the largest effect at the top, and the heatmap is on the right with one
column per level. A long meta-analysis then grows downwards, which suits
scrolling and portrait pages. All the examples use the `forestmap_example`
data that comes with the package.

## Turning the plot

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c(
    "Population" = "population",
    "Outcome measure" = "outcome",
    "Study design" = "design",
    "Country" = "country",
    "Sample size" = "n"
  ),
  orientation = "vertical",
  y_label = "SMD (95% CI)"
)
```

Each property's levels are labelled above their columns, and the property's
name is centred above those. A numeric property, here sample size, gets one
column labelled with its name in bold, with bars growing to the right. Long
names are wrapped onto two lines when their columns are narrow; put `\n` in
a name to choose where it breaks, e.g. `"Outcome\nmeasure" = "outcome"`.
This applies only to the names above categorical columns: a numeric
property's name is its column's label, which stays on one line and ignores
`\n`.

`forest_height` sets the forest plot's share of the *width* in this
layout, e.g. `forest_height = 0.5` for equal halves.

## Study names

Give a column of study names with `study`, and each row is labelled:

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c(
    "Population" = "population",
    "Outcome measure" = "outcome",
    "Study design" = "design",
    "Country" = "country",
    "Sample size" = "n"
  ),
  orientation = "vertical",
  study = "study",
  y_label = "SMD (95% CI)"
)
```

## When labels are cramped

With many studies or levels, labels can crowd each other. Three settings
help.

`label_size` sets the size, in points, of each kind of label: `study` for
study names, `level` for the levels above the columns, and `moderator` for
property names. Any you leave out follow `text_size`.

`level_angle` sets the angle of the level labels, from 0 (flat) to 90
(upright). Upright labels take less width.

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c(
    "Population" = "population",
    "Outcome measure" = "outcome",
    "Study design" = "design",
    "Country" = "country",
    "Sample size" = "n"
  ),
  orientation = "vertical",
  study = "study",
  label_size = c(study = 6, level = 7, moderator = 8),
  level_angle = 90,
  y_label = "SMD (95% CI)"
)
```

Finally, give the plot more room when you save it. A vertical plot needs
roughly 0.15 inches of height per study:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ggplot2::ggsave("forestmap.png", p, width = 7, height = 9.5, dpi = 300)
```

## Everything else works the same

Every other option works in the vertical layout too: palettes, `rope`,
`null_value`, `max_levels`, and the styles and ranges of numeric
properties. With `continuous_range = "end"`, the range key sits under the
property's column:

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Sample size" = "n"),
  orientation = "vertical",
  study = "study",
  continuous_style = "tint",
  continuous_range = "end",
  rope = 0.1,
  palette = "okabe_ito"
)
```
